rationale: Systems chosen for closed-form analysis are a biased, often simple sample, but complete analysis does not imply simple behavior: the doubling map and the logistic map at full chaos have exact solutions yet are chaotic. The universal claim that analyzability yields only simple behavior is therefore too strong.

Because the base-2 logarithm of 3 is irrational, n times that logarithm is equidistributed mod 1, which forces the leading binary digits of 3^n to behave like a random sequence, and computed blocks show only short-range structure from the multiplication carries. Apparent practical randomness is well supported even though normality is not proved.

Computed fractional parts of successive powers of 3/2 fluctuate irregularly, in line with the digits of those powers. Density of this sequence in the unit interval is still an open problem, so the appearance of randomness is empirical rather than a theorem, but it holds across the ranges that have been calculated.

Piecewise maps built from multiplication and halving, of which the Collatz map is the best-known relative, produce integer trajectories whose magnitudes wander irregularly for enormously long stretches with no observed cycle. The existential claim is well supported computationally, though global absence of eventual repetition is rarely proved.

Carries really are non-local while cellular-automaton updates are local, and both families do show the same broad menu of periodic, nested, chaotic, and localized behavior. Rule details still decide which kind appears, so the further claim that those details do not matter is only partly right.

Binary reverse-and-add from a power of two produces digit plots with particle-like streaks over long computed windows, and no short repeating regime is seen. That is an observation about a finite run of one seed, not a proof that the pattern never becomes periodic.

Nested recursions such as the Hofstadter Q-sequence and related meta-Fibonacci sequences use only earlier terms combined by addition, yet their graphs fluctuate irregularly and pass many statistical checks for randomness. Existence of such examples is solid even where proofs of chaoticity are lacking.

The sieve is simple, but prime gaps, residue biases, and pair correlations closely track models that treat primes as random integers with the prime-number density. Modular constraints and the zeta zeros are real structure, which is why the claim correctly says 'in many respects' rather than in every respect.

Many elementary number-theoretic sequences remain intractable, and primes are the clearest case of complexity generated by a short rule. Several listed families are solved and highly structured, such as sums of two or four squares, and identifying that complexity with cellular-automaton complexity is an interpretation rather than an established equivalence.

Huge computed prefixes of pi in the bases that have actually been generated pass standard statistical batteries with no persistent pattern. Normality in every base is unproved, but the claim is about practical randomness of the digits that have been computed, which the evidence supports.

In any integer base, a real number has an eventually periodic expansion if and only if it is rational, and for a reduced denominator q the repetend length is the multiplicative order of the base modulo the part of q coprime to the base, hence at most q-1. This is a standard theorem.

Digits of square roots of small non-squares, and of many larger ones that have been expanded, are statistically indistinguishable from random sequences. The claim is hedged by 'as far as can be determined' and does not require the unproved normality of every quadratic irrational.

Cube roots of non-cubes, logarithms of small integers, and exponentials such as e have digit sequences that pass the same randomness tests as square roots, with only the obvious exceptions of perfect powers. 'Almost all' of the simple cases matches what has been computed.

Digit sequences generated by substitution systems are automatic or morphic and have very low block complexity, while an algebraic irrational, including any integer root that is not an integer, cannot have an automatic base-b expansion. The theorem covers the standard nested sequences; a few exotic morphic cases are less completely settled.

Quadratic irrationals, including square roots of non-squares, have eventually periodic continued fractions, and e has an explicit regular pattern of partial quotients. Partial quotients of pi and of higher-degree roots such as cube roots show no such pattern and match the statistics expected of a generic continued fraction.

Incompressibility of long digit blocks changes only mildly when the base changes, and pi looks irregular in both digits and continued fractions, so representation is not the whole story. Other numbers, notably square roots, look complex in one representation and simple in another, which is why the claim is only 'often' true.

The zeros of sin(x)+sin(αx) fall into two arithmetic progressions whose spacing ratio is (α-1)/(α+1), so the interleaving is a mechanical word governed by that number's continued fraction. Quadratic α makes the continued fraction periodic and the zero pattern substitutive, which is the nested case.

The doubling map shifts the binary expansion one place, so each output digit is a digit that was already present in the seed. It amplifies ignorance of the seed but does not create algorithmic randomness from a simple initial number.

The map taking the fractional part of 3x/2, started at 1/2, produces an irregular computable orbit whose complexity is not stored as random digits of the seed. Calling that 'intrinsic randomness' is a phenomenological description; the orbit remains a short deterministic program and is not random in the algorithmic sense.

Sensitive dependence stretches differences that are already in the initial state or in external noise; by itself it does not add new bits. The wording is strict, but the separation between amplification and genuine production of randomness is the right one for deterministic maps.

Coupled map lattices and other continuous-valued cellular automata with simple local averaging maps produce spatiotemporal chaos and coherent localized structures. The match with discrete cellular automata is qualitative but repeatedly observed.

Tractability mattered in the history of modeling, but continuum equations were adopted because fields, fluids, and elasticity are approximately continuous, including equations that had no closed solution. An earlier arrival of computers would have added discrete models without displacing partial differential equations as the default for those phenomena.

Maxwell's equations, the Schrödinger equation, and classical general relativity are effective theories, each known to fail outside its regime, so nature does not fundamentally follow those particular equations. Whether the replacement is still a continuum theory remains open, but the claim as aimed at these models is well supported.

Simple nonlinear partial differential equations, notably the Kuramoto–Sivashinsky equation, produce sustained spatiotemporal chaos. Reports of apparently discrete patches inside such equations are more fragile, because coarse grids can imitate cellular automata, so that part of the claim is less secure.

Exact iteration makes complexity easy to see in discrete systems, whereas continuous systems add truncation error, and that methodological gap is real. Comparable complexity is already seen in ordinary differential equations, partial differential equations, and coupled maps, which supports the claim that it is not fundamentally rarer.

Periodic, chaotic, fractal, and localized behavior, and even Turing-universal simulation, all occur in some continuous systems with compact descriptions. 'Essentially all' phenomena of discrete simple programs is a broader conjecture than those examples establish.

One-dimensional cellular automata, Turing machines, and substitution systems already exhibit nested, chaotic, and localized complex behavior, so extra dimensions are not required for complexity to occur. Higher dimensions add new geometric effects, but within this class of systems they do not change the basic occurrence of complexity.

One-dimensional cuts through the evolution of two-dimensional totalistic cellular automata often look like ordinary one-dimensional automata, with the same mix of periodic, nested, and disordered texture. A slice is not itself a closed one-dimensional rule, because off-slice neighbors influence it, so the resemblance is visual rather than exact.

Certain outer-totalistic rules on the square lattice have growth speeds that vary little with direction, and the resulting blobs stay close to circular over large radii. The limiting shape of a finite-range lattice rule is typically not a mathematically perfect circle, which the claim does not require.

The irreversible exactly-three-of-eight growth rule can produce outlines that look irregular for a long time, so complexity of overall shape is real as a finite-time phenomenon. Monotone lattice growth often settles into a polygonal limiting shape, so 'keeps changing with no simple form' may fail asymptotically.

Three-dimensional cellular automata display the same broad behavioral kinds already seen in one and two dimensions, including disorder and localized structures, along with some genuinely new geometric effects. That supports the conclusion that complexity is not an artifact of one particular dimension.

Small two-dimensional Turing machines, like one-dimensional ones, tend to show only periodic or nested behavior until the head has enough states for rarer irregular motion. The specific rate of a few complex rules per million at four states is a sampling result that is plausible but not independently established here.

If every element is replaced from its own type alone, the construction is a substitution system or an iterated function system and is self-similar at every stage. That forces a nested structure even when overlaps make the picture look busy.

Context-free geometric replacements are nested because parts do not interact, and neighbor-dependent grid substitutions do produce non-nested patterns. Traditional fractal geometry also includes Julia sets, diffusion-limited aggregates, and random fractals, which are not purely nested, so the claim about all of its patterns is too broad.

A directed grid in two dimensions can be drawn with exactly two outgoing links per node, and trees and nested graphs are easy at that degree. Higher-dimensional arrays need gadget-like clusters of nodes rather than a literal grid of out-degree two, but those encodings exist, so the existence claim is reasonable.

Rules that see only whether the two outgoing links coincide are too weak to do much besides regular growth, while a slightly larger neighborhood can encode irregular insertion of nodes. The quoted frequency of about one irregular rule in 10,000 is a specific census figure that may be right but is not a structural theorem.

Discrete network models of spacetime are serious research programs, but none has been shown to reproduce observed spacetime, and continuum field theory remains the working fundamental framework. The claim that such systems will likely turn out to be the structure of our spacetime is a conjecture, not a supported likelihood.

Simple multiway rewriting systems typically either terminate or branch by a roughly constant factor per step, because each string has a fixed set of rewrites. Intermediate, slow growth requires special cancellation or confluence and is empirically uncommon.

Slowly growing multiway systems that can be run to completion often fall into long cycles, and a period of 1071 steps is a concrete reported example. 'Typically' is only as strong as the sample of systems small enough to exhaust, so later aperiodic slow growth is not ruled out.

A fixed rewrite rule sends each string to a fixed set of successors, so the evolution is exactly a directed graph of states, and those graphs are often highly branched. This is true by the definition of a multiway system.

A one-dimensional local constraint corresponds to a finite graph of allowed adjacent blocks, and any infinite allowed coloring gives an infinite path, which in a finite graph must contain a cycle. That cycle is a purely periodic global arrangement, so satisfiable one-dimensional local constraints cannot force an aperiodic pattern.

There are exactly 2^32 subsets of the 32 possible two-color von Neumann templates, and for this tiny alphabet aperiodicity is not expected, unlike larger tiling problems. The precise counts of unsatisfiable rules and of 171 sufficient periodic patterns are census results that are credible but easy to get wrong by an off-by-one in the search.

An evolution rule can be iterated forward, whereas a constraint system only defines an allowed set, and finding a member can require search. In two dimensions that search is in general undecidable, so the computational contrast is genuine even though some special constraints are easy.

Ordering simple template constraints and finding that the first one incompatible with every periodic coloring forces a unique nested pattern is a definite computational claim, and nested self-similarity is a plausible minimal aperiodic solution. The exact index 18762389 stands or falls with one enumeration and is only moderately corroborated.

The stated search space size 2^37 is the right count for template constraints with one required pattern, and a search of millions that finds nothing beyond nested behavior is a limited negative report. The claim does not say no more complex example exists outside the ones tested.

Spacetime diagrams of a cellular automaton are tilings: 3×3 allowed blocks can enforce a local update rule together with a fixed initial row, and rule 30's diagram is largely disordered. A construction with 56 allowed templates is a specific encoding that is plausible and standard in method, though the exact count is a design choice.

Complex cellular-automaton rules are easy to find by sampling, whereas forcing aperiodicity or randomness by a short list of local constraints took landmark constructions and large alphabets. Exhaustive checks of small template families agree that almost all satisfiable simple constraints still allow a periodic pattern.

Equilibrium and constraint thinking did favor simple closed-form solutions, and complicated constraints are indeed needed to force complicated patterns. Traditional mathematics nevertheless identified chaos, turbulence, and fractals, so constraint-style equations did not in fact prevent the recognition of complexity.

From random initial data, many cellular automata relax to uniform or periodic states, and others, such as the Game of Life, condense random soup into still lifes, oscillators, and gliders. Spontaneous appearance of distinctly non-random structure is a standard, repeatedly observed fact.

The four classes—dying out, settling into simple persistent structures, sustained disorder, and interacting localized structures—are the usual working classification of cellular automata started from random data. Borderline rules exist, but almost all common rules are easy to place.

Class 4, as seen in the Game of Life and rule 110, is defined by localized structures that are simple in isolation yet collide in complicated ways. That description matches the systems the class was introduced to name.

Damage spreading, entropy, and transient length do correlate with the visual classes, so the class is often a useful predictor. Within a class the variation is large, and additive disordered rules differ sharply from nonlinear ones, so class membership does not determine most detailed properties.

Which behavioral class a rule falls into is undecidable in general, and in practice one simulates the rule. Special forms, including nilpotent and some linear rules, can be proved to stay in the simple classes, exactly as the claim allows.

Class 4 activity neither collapses as in class 2 nor stays uniformly high as in class 3, and in one-parameter families such rules often sit near the ordered-to-chaotic transition. The transition picture is statistical rather than a sharp law for every rule ordering.

Continuous-state cellular automata, as a parameter is varied, pass through quiescent, periodic, disordered, and intermittent regimes with localized structures near the transitions. The analogy with the four discrete classes is close, though the boundaries are smoother.

Slices of two-dimensional cellular automata show the same four phenomenological classes, and the Game of Life is the standard class 4 example. Class 4 growth on an otherwise white background does occur for some rules slightly richer than Life, which needs a nontrivial seed.

A single-cell change typically dies in class 1, remains local in class 2, spreads in a widening cone in class 3, and spreads intermittently in class 4. Those are characteristic diagnostics, with exceptions among rules near class boundaries.

Matching a natural system to forgetting, local storage, or long-range signaling is sometimes a useful analogy, as with crystals versus turbulence. It is not, by itself, enough to understand the most important features of natural systems across the board.

A deterministic system with finitely many discrete states must eventually repeat a full state, after which the trajectory cycles, and the cycle length cannot exceed the number of states. This is the pigeonhole principle.

In class 2 the influence of a cell stays within a bounded region, so each patch is effectively a finite automaton and must cycle, usually with a short period. 'Always' and 'a few cells' describe the typical case; the effective width and period can be larger for some rules still called class 2.

On a ring, class 3 elementary rules tend to have cycle lengths that grow rapidly and unevenly with the ring size. Singling out rule 45 as the only rule whose periods stay near the maximum for every size is a stronger survey claim than the general class 3 pattern, and other chaotic elementary rules also have very long cycles.

Rule 30 and rule 22, started from a single black cell, produce long disordered patterns that pass statistical tests, so the randomness is not copied from a random initial condition. The sequences are still computable, but the claim is about phenomenological randomness, which the examples support.

Rule 90 is linear over the field with two elements, so its evolution is the superposition of nested single-seed patterns and a sparse initial defect never thermalizes. Rule 22 is nonlinear and empirically forgets a low initial density, which is the contrast the claim draws.

Rule 30 and rule 22 look statistically similar from many disordered or simple seeds, which is a real form of stability. They do not do so for every initial condition—the blank state and some short spatially periodic states stay regular—and the leap to the stability of natural systems is an analogy.

A spatially periodic initial condition stays spatially periodic under a cellular automaton, and the repeating block then evolves as a finite deterministic system, so the time behavior eventually repeats. The stated cap of 2^n is correct for two colors and false for more colors, where the same block can have a period as long as the full number of colorings.

Blocking or sublattice encodings are common: rule 126 on suitably paired cells reproduces rule 90, and other class 3 rules have special backgrounds on which they behave like class 2. 'Common' is an empirical statement about how often such seeds turn up, and they do turn up often.

If blocks evolve by the same rule as single cells, the spacetime diagram is built by repeating one pattern at every scale, which yields a uniform or nested configuration. That is the mechanism behind rule 90 and the rules that emulate it.

Linearity lets an additive rule reproduce itself on scaled blocks, and from simple seeds the result is nested; among two-color nearest-neighbor rules, 90 and 150 are the basic genuinely two-sided examples. One-sided additive rules such as the shift and rule 60 are further cases, and rule 184 is a plausible but less central non-additive example of self-emulation.

The strings still present after t steps of a one-dimensional cellular automaton form a regular language whose automaton stays small or grows only polynomially for typical class 1 and 2 rules and explodes for many class 3 and 4 rules. Surjective rules started from every possible string are the stated exception, because every string remains possible; the specific t^2 growth is typical rather than universal.

If every localized structure eventually died, a class 4 evolution would fall into a uniform or simply periodic regime, so some forever-persistent structures are part of what the class means. That most structures die is typical of random initial data in Life-like rules, not a separate theorem.

In studied class 4 rules, once persistent structures are rich enough, gliders or other moving patterns are eventually found, and motion is what carries signals between collisions. The 'whenever' is experience from many rules rather than a proof that stationary structures alone cannot be complicated.

Some class 4 rules, including rule 110 and the Game of Life, are computationally universal and can be set up to grow either complicated or very simple unbounded patterns. Universality is not established for class 4 rules in general, so it is not yet a general feature of the class.

The persistent structures of rule 110 are individually periodic, but their collisions emit new structures and can take huge numbers of steps to resolve, which is the concrete mechanism behind its ability to simulate arbitrary computation. The same collision cascades are seen in other class 4 rules such as Life.

Across many simple programs the same few behavioral kinds recur, so some universality of behavior is real. Extending that to the claim that idealized cell models and real molecular systems must share the same features, regardless of underlying details, goes beyond what the experiments show.

External noise, randomness already present in the initial state, and randomness generated by the evolution itself cover the usual sources of apparent randomness in classical systems. The list is less clearly exhaustive once irreducible quantum randomness is included, and the boundaries among the three mechanisms are not sharp.
